At p4-examples: Add four short opening items: (a) Find two integers with product 24 and sum 11. (b) Find two integers with product −30 and sum −13. (c) Factorise x(2x+3)+4(2x+3). (d) Factorise 6x²+x−2 using splitting and grouping. Answers: (a) 3 and 8; (b) −15 and 2; (c) (x+4)(2x+3); (d) (3x+2)(2x−1). Keep the review within one page.

[Pedagogy review · Suggestion · extension · pf-28099eba10]
As a follow-up to p11-q9-a after Question 10: (i) Solve x⁶−13x³+36=0 using u=x³. Answer: x=∛4 or ∛9. (ii) Explain why this equation has two real solutions while Question 9a has four. Answer: each positive cube gives one real cube root; each positive square gives two signed square roots.

[Pedagogy review · Suggestion · extension · pf-aa76bcc349]
After p7-q3-e, add parts: (f) Solve x(x−1)(x+2)=0. Answer: x=0,1,−2. (g) Solve (x−1)²(x+2)=0. Answer: x=1,−2. (h) Explain why (f) and (g) have different numbers of distinct solutions. Answer: the factor x supplies the additional root 0, whereas the repeated factor x−1 supplies the existing root 1.

[Pedagogy review · Suggestion · extension · pf-b6347150cc]
At p26-q6-response: Add a follow-up to Q6, attempted after p27 teaching: (a) For k=16, fully factorise both expressions. Answers: (x+2)(x+8) and (x−2)(x−8). (b) For k=25, write both expressions as perfect squares. Answers: (x+5)² and (x−5)². (c) For k=26, can either expression be factorised into real linear factors? Explain why. Answer: neither; the completed forms are (x+5)²+1 and (x−5)²+1, which are strictly positive for every real x.
